passage.bullet: Royal Society voyage officially carried Joseph Banks to Tahiti → observed Venus crossing the Sun
Sealed Admiralty orders commanded Cook south into uncharted waters → searched for Terra Australis
Instructed to claim southern territories for King George III → beat rival European empires

context.bullet: Britain and France competed globally after 1763 → Pacific exploration served imperial expansion
Admiralty instructions required local consent before claiming inhabited land → Cook later ignored this

stems.stem: Officially, HMS Endeavour sailed to Tahiti so ____________ could record the ____________.
Once that astronomical task ended, locked ____________ ordered Cook south to find ____________.
The British Crown wanted this territory claimed for ____________ before ____________ could seize it.

lesson_1.watch_out: HMS Endeavour was not purely a peaceful science mission—Cook carried sealed naval orders for imperial annexation.

passage.bullet: Tahitian high priest Tupaia read stars, swells, birds, and clouds → guided Endeavour without instruments
Drafted a sweeping Pacific chart plotting over 130 islands → filled vast gaps in European maps
Shared Polynesian linguistic roots with Māori communities → acted as vital translator in New Zealand

context.bullet: Eighteenth-century British naval charts left most of the South Pacific blank → Indigenous expertise proved essential
Polynesian navigators had crossed open Pacific oceans for centuries → passed wayfinding down orally

stems.stem: Without reliable European maps, Cook relied on ____________, who navigated using ____________ rather than instruments.
Drawing on ancestral Pacific knowledge, this Arioi priest charted over ____________ across thousands of miles.
When the expedition reached New Zealand, his shared language roots allowed him to ____________ with ____________.

lesson_1.watch_out: Cook did not navigate the South Pacific unaided—Tahitian master navigator Tupaia provided crucial wayfinding and diplomacy.

passage.bullet: Two Gweagal warriors of the Dharawal nation brandished spears → followed defensive protocol to forbid landing
Cook treated territorial defence as hostility and fired muskets → wounded one warrior in the leg
Warriors retreated behind coastal dunes → British landing party came ashore through armed force

context.bullet: First Nations clans had governed coastal country for 65,000 years → entry required customary permission
Cook’s crew seized spears and a bark shield after the clash → shipped to London museums

stems.stem: As British rowing boats neared the shore in April 1770, two ____________ shouted warnings to ____________.
Misreading customary boundary defence as aggression, Cook ordered ____________, leaving one defender ____________.
Once the defenders pulled back behind the dunes, the British stepped ashore under ____________ rather than welcome.

lesson_1.watch_out: Gweagal warriors were not launching an unprovoked attack—they were enforcing ancient legal protocols protecting Dharawal country.

passage.bullet: Hoisted the Union Jack on Possession Island → claimed eastern Australia for King George III
Admiralty orders permitted claiming inhabited lands only with native consent → Cook sought zero Indigenous agreement
Four months sailing north had revealed campfires and coastal peoples → proved the continent was inhabited

context.bullet: Gweagal warriors had already resisted Cook’s landing in April → directly disproved any willing consent
Unlike British treaties signed later in New Zealand → eastern Australia was claimed without Indigenous negotiation

stems.stem: In August 1770, Cook landed off Cape York, raised ____________, and claimed the eastern coast for ____________.
This ceremony directly broke his Admiralty orders, which stated inhabited land required ____________.
Having encountered warriors at ____________ and sighted peoples along the coast, Cook knew the land was ____________.

lesson_1.watch_out: Cook never claimed the entire continent at Botany Bay—he claimed the eastern coast months later on Possession Island.

passage.bullet: British law equated land ownership with fences, iron ploughs, and towns → dismissed Indigenous custodianship
Jurists declared the continent terra nullius, land belonging to nobody → erased First Nations legal sovereignty
Crown refused to sign treaties with clan elders → triggered two centuries of uncompensated dispossession

context.bullet: Over 250 Indigenous nations actively managed country through fire-stick farming → contradicted Cook’s nomad myth
Terra nullius stood in Australian law until 1992 → overturned at last by Eddie Mabo’s case

stems.stem: Relying on flawed accounts, British jurists judged ownership by European markers such as ____________ and ____________.
Classifying Australia as ____________ meant the Crown treated inhabited country as land belonging to ____________.
Consequently, Britain negotiated zero ____________ with clan elders and stripped First Nations peoples of ____________.

lesson_1.watch_out: Terra nullius did not mean the British saw zero people—it meant European law refused to recognise Indigenous land ownership.

passage.bullet: American independence in 1783 ended transatlantic convict transportation → triggered an urgent British prison crisis
Harsh property laws packed rotting Thames prison hulks → bred deadly typhus and dangerous overcrowding
Prime Minister William Pitt selected distant Botany Bay → exported convicts far from London

context.bullet: Joseph Banks promoted Botany Bay after the 1770 voyage → persuaded Parliament to colonise eastern Australia
Settling New South Wales also secured Pacific trade routes → countered rival French naval ambitions

stems.stem: Defeat in the 1783 War of Independence stopped Britain transporting convicted felons to ____________.
Meanwhile, harsh ____________ convictions crammed minor offenders onto rotting ____________, where ____________ spread rapidly.
To relieve overflowing jails, Prime Minister ____________ ordered a new penal settlement at ____________.

lesson_2.watch_out: Most transported convicts were petty urban thieves convicted under the Bloody Code, not hardened violent murderers.

passage.bullet: Governor Arthur Phillip enforced strict shipboard hygiene and deck ventilation → curbed deadly typhus outbreaks
Resupplied across 15,000 miles at Rio de Janeiro and Cape Town → kept drinking water fresh
Fewer than fifty died across eleven ships → remarkable survival for an eight-month ocean voyage

context.bullet: Private contractors ran the 1790 Second Fleet for profit → starved convicts suffered catastrophic death rates
Many convicts boarded already weakened from disease-ridden Thames hulks → made Phillip’s low mortality extraordinary

stems.stem: Commanding eleven ships across 15,000 miles, Captain ____________ insisted on strict ____________ and ____________ below decks.
Calling at ports such as ____________ and ____________ ensured convicts received clean ____________ during the eight-month crossing.
Through these precautions, fewer than ____________ out of over 750 convicts perished before reaching Australia.

lesson_2.watch_out: Do not confuse the carefully managed First Fleet with later private convict fleets—Phillip’s strict naval care kept deaths unusually low.

passage.bullet: Botany Bay had shallow water, exposed anchorage, and swampy ground → lacked a reliable freshwater river
Scouting north revealed Port Jackson’s deep, sheltered harbour → protected tall ships from ocean storms
Sydney Cove offered a flowing freshwater stream → enabled permanent camp foundation on 26 January 1788

context.bullet: Cook visited briefly in autumn 1770 → missed how dry Botany Bay became in January
Sydney Cove was Warrane, heartland of the Gadigal clan → British landing dispossessed Eora custodians

stems.stem: Upon arriving in January 1788, Phillip rejected Botany Bay due to its ____________, swampy soil, and lack of ____________.
Scouting north into ____________, he discovered deep-water anchorages capable of sheltering the entire fleet.
Phillip selected ____________ because a dependable ____________ ran directly into the sheltered bay.

lesson_2.watch_out: The First Fleet anchored first at Botany Bay, not Sydney Harbour—Phillip relocated north after finding Botany Bay unsuitable.

passage.bullet: Urban convicts lacked farming skills and planted spoiled English seed in sandy soil → crops failed
Cheap iron hoes and axes snapped against dense hardwood roots → stalled land clearing
HMS Guardian struck an Antarctic iceberg carrying relief stores → forced drastic ration cuts

context.bullet: Colonists dismissed Eora yams, bush foods, and fishing methods → starved beside thriving Indigenous ecosystems
Phillip shipped hundreds of convicts to fertile Norfolk Island → eased pressure on Sydney’s food stores

stems.stem: Agricultural production collapsed early on because urban convicts lacked ____________ and Sydney’s ____________ ruined English grain.
Clearing the bush proved agonisingly slow as poor-quality ____________ shattered on tough native tree roots.
Crisis deepened when relief ship ____________ hit an iceberg, forcing Phillip to ____________ and send people to ____________.

lesson_2.watch_out: Sydney’s soil was not completely barren everywhere—British settlers tried using European crops and weak tools unsuited to Australian conditions.

passage.bullet: Convicts quarried stone and cleared bush all day → built Sydney’s early roads and storehouses
Guards flogged offenders with the cat-o'-nine-tails for drunkenness or insolence → enforced strict penal order
Freed emancipists like James Ruse received 30-acre Rose Hill farms → achieved vital grain self-sufficiency

context.bullet: Early Sydney lacked stone prison walls → relied on rations, flogging, and tickets-of-leave for control
Fertile emancipist farms around Rose Hill pushed inland → encroached directly onto Dharug hunting country

stems.stem: To maintain penal order, guards enforced dawn-to-dusk labour and punished misconduct with the ____________.
Alongside punishment, Phillip offered ____________ to hardworking ____________ once their sentences expired.
At Rose Hill, former convict ____________ harvested wheat and corn, moving the colony toward ____________.

lesson_2.watch_out: Emancipists were pardoned or time-served former convicts—unlike free settlers, they earned land after enduring transportation.

passage.bullet: Practised deliberate fire-stick farming across dry grasslands → prevented destructive bushfires and regenerated wallaby grazing
Over 250 language nations stewarded defined ancestral lands → sustained ecosystems from Eora coast to desert
Ancient Songlines wove Dreaming stories, customary law, and navigation → bound clans to care for country

context.bullet: Park-like pastures admired by British arrivals were human-made → directly refuted the myth of untouched wilderness
Clans belonged to sacred country rather than owning private plots → clashed with British enclosures

stems.stem: Across more than 250 language nations, communities used ____________ to clear dry scrub and encourage fresh ____________.
Spiritual tracks known as ____________ linked Dreaming stories, navigational routes, and ____________ across the continent.
Through these custodial practices, First Nations peoples sustained the world’s oldest ____________ for over ____________.

lesson_3.watch_out: Fire-stick farming was careful, seasonal ecological engineering—never confuse it with random or uncontrolled bushfires.

passage.bullet: Lacking biological immunity to gal-galla smallpox → 50 to 70 percent of Eora people died
Mass deaths of senior elders destroyed oral law and sacred stories → fractured clan governance
Survivors fled infected harbour camps in terror → crippled Eora capacity to resist British expansion

context.bullet: British netting and tree-felling had already depleted Eora food sources → worsened vulnerability before April 1789
First Fleet surgeons carried variolous smallpox matter in glass bottles → origin remains fiercely debated

stems.stem: Because First Nations communities possessed zero prior immunity, the April 1789 ____________ outbreak killed ____________ of Eora people.
Losing senior ____________ proved devastating because sacred law, history, and ecological knowledge were preserved orally.
As grieving survivors fled ____________, local clans were left severely weakened against expanding British settlement.

lesson_3.watch_out: Smallpox did not merely reduce population numbers—losing elders destroyed living libraries of oral law and ceremony.

passage.bullet: Kidnapped on Phillip’s orders in 1789 → learned English and mediated between Eora clans and colonists
Sailed with Phillip to England in 1792 → returned to Sydney after colonial attitudes hardened
Dismissed by later British officials yet estranged from traditional kin → left isolated between two cultures

context.bullet: Bennelong sought peaceful coexistence after the 1789 epidemic → hoped diplomacy might protect Wangal kin
Phillip built him a brick harbourside hut → site where the Sydney Opera House now stands

stems.stem: Kidnapped by marines in 1789, Wangal man ____________ learned English and served as a ____________ for Governor Phillip.
Even after travelling to ____________ in 1792, he returned to a colony growing increasingly hostile toward Indigenous people.
Shunned by new ____________ and distanced from ____________, he spent his later years caught between two worlds.

lesson_3.watch_out: Bennelong was not a passive collaborator—initially kidnapped by force, he used diplomacy strategically to navigate invasion.

passage.bullet: United Bidjigal and neighbouring Sydney Basin clans → waged coordinated guerrilla campaigns against colonial expansion
Burned settler crops, raided grain stores, and speared livestock → starved outlying British farms
Fought redcoats at Parramatta in 1797 and escaped hospital wounded → became a legendary resistance symbol

context.bullet: Spears could not match musket volleys in open fields → hit-and-run bush ambushes neutralised British firepower
Expanding convict and emancipist farms around Parramatta → seized Bidjigal hunting grounds and provoked retaliation

stems.stem: Rejecting colonial expansion, Bidjigal leader ____________ united Sydney clans to launch ____________ against outlying settlements.
Warriors struck the colony’s food supply directly by burning ____________ and spearing stolen or grazing ____________.
During the 1797 ____________, he survived severe gunshot wounds and escaped captivity, cementing his ____________.

lesson_3.watch_out: Frontier resistance was organised economic warfare—Pemulwuy deliberately targeted crops and cattle to halt farm expansion.

passage.bullet: Hawkesbury farms fenced off Dharug yam beds and fishing reaches → sparked fierce raids on homesteads
Governor King issued shoot-on-sight orders against Indigenous warriors → legalised killing Aboriginal people without trial
Pemulwuy was shot in an 1802 ambush and decapitated → ended Sydney’s first organised frontier war

context.bullet: Rich Hawkesbury alluvial soil fed hungry Sydney → pushed governors to crush Dharug resistance ruthlessly
Pemulwuy’s remains were sent to Joseph Banks in England → descendants still campaign for repatriation

stems.stem: Conflict intensified along the ____________ when British farms cut Dharug families off from vital ____________ and fishing waters.
To crush the raids, Governor ____________ outlawed warriors and authorised settlers to ____________ without trial.
Organised resistance collapsed in 1802 after ____________ was killed in an ambush and his head was sent to ____________.

lesson_3.watch_out: Early Australian colonisation was never peaceful settlement—governors deployed redcoats and shoot-on-sight decrees in open frontier war.

passage.bullet: Soldiers fired cannon and muskets on peaceful Palawa kangaroo hunters in 1804 → shattered early relations
Pastoralists overran fertile Tasmanian Midlands grasslands with sheep → destroyed essential Palawa kangaroo hunting grounds
Convict stockmen and sealers kidnapped Aboriginal women → provoked two decades of fierce retaliatory warfare

context.bullet: Napoleonic rivalry pushed Britain to occupy Van Diemen’s Land in 1803 → blocked French claims
Unlike mainland clans, Tasmania’s 6,000 Palawa lived on a bounded island → left nowhere to retreat

stems.stem: Bloodshed began in May 1804 when nervous troops fired ____________ at three hundred Palawa families on a ____________.
Over the next twenty years, sheep farmers seized the ____________, starving clans of traditional food sources.
Widespread settler abuses, including the ____________ of Palawa women, drove clans into sustained guerrilla retaliation.

lesson_4.watch_out: The 1804 Risdon Cove killings were unprovoked—the Palawa group included women and children conducting a seasonal kangaroo drive.

passage.bullet: Palawa warriors knew rugged Tasmanian forests intimately → slipped silently through gaps in the cordon
Rough terrain, thick scrub, and foul weather broke up the 2,200-man line → created wide openings
Seven weeks and £30,000 yielded just two captives → exposed British military failure against guerrilla tactics

context.bullet: Governor Arthur had already suspended civilian law in 1828 → licensed roving parties to kill Palawa
Although tactically defeated, the vast mobilisation signalled relentless settler numbers → pushed exhausted clans toward negotiation

stems.stem: After declaring martial law in 1828, Governor Arthur deployed ____________ in October 1830 to sweep Palawa clans toward ____________.
Using superior knowledge of Tasmania’s ____________, Palawa families slipped straight past the slow-moving British cordon.
Despite spending ____________ over seven weeks, the operation captured only ____________, proving conventional sweeps ineffective.

lesson_4.watch_out: Martial law in 1828 meant Palawa people—nominally claimed as British subjects—were legally treated as an enemy army to be shot.

passage.bullet: Truganini helped Robinson negotiate peace expecting temporary sanctuary → authorities instead imposed permanent Flinders Island exile
Gales, respiratory disease, and salted rations plagued Wybalenna → over 150 of 200 exiles died
Mission rules banned traditional ceremony and language → deepened grief and homesickness for ancestral country

context.bullet: Settlers had murdered Truganini’s close kin → drove her desperate diplomatic effort to save survivors
Colonial writers falsely claimed Tasmanian Aboriginal people became extinct → Palawa descendants still thrive today

stems.stem: Hoping to save surviving clans, Nuenonne woman ____________ accompanied missionary ____________ to negotiate safe protection.
Breaking those promises, colonial officials shipped around two hundred Palawa to damp, windswept ____________ on ____________.
Malnutrition, homesickness, and ____________ killed more than ____________ captives there within a single decade.

lesson_4.watch_out: Never repeat the nineteenth-century colonial myth that Truganini’s death meant Palawa extinction—Tasmanian Aboriginal communities endure today.

passage.bullet: Booming Yorkshire textile mills hungered for fine Merino fleece → made Australian sheep grazing hugely profitable
Wealthy squatters drove millions of sheep beyond the Blue Mountains → seized vast Indigenous plains
Hard-hoofed flocks trampled yam daisy beds and fouled waterholes → forced starving clans to spear sheep

context.bullet: Australian squatters were rich pastoralists occupying Crown land illegally → later gained powerful political dominance
Absence of Indigenous treaties let pastoralists claim open grasslands freely → rapidly widened mainland frontier wars

stems.stem: Industrialisation in Britain fuelled intense ____________ for fine wool, turning ____________ flocks into immense colonial wealth.
Crossing the Blue Mountains, pastoralists known as ____________ fenced off sacred ____________ and occupied vast inland runs.
As grazing sheep crushed native ____________, hungry Aboriginal clans retaliated by ____________, sparking fierce frontier violence.

lesson_4.watch_out: In colonial Australia, squatters were not poor homeless settlers—they were wealthy wool barons seizing vast inland estates.

passage.bullet: Stockmen slaughtered twenty-eight peaceful Wirrayaraay elders, women, and children → burned bodies to hide evidence
Governor Gipps pursued two Sydney trials → seven white perpetrators were hanged for murdering Aboriginal people
Furious squatter backlash drove frontier violence underground → settlers used poison and secrecy to evade prosecution

context.bullet: Station overseer William Hobbs reported the charred remains despite threats → made legal prosecution possible
Hundreds of frontier massacres occurred across Australia → almost no other white killers ever faced execution

stems.stem: At Myall Creek in June 1838, armed stockmen murdered twenty-eight unresisting ____________ people and burned their remains.
Backed by Governor ____________, a second Sydney trial ended with ____________ being executed—an unprecedented legal ruling.
Rather than ending frontier killings, angry ____________ responded with a code of ____________ to conceal future massacres.

lesson_4.watch_out: Myall Creek did not end frontier massacres—instead, settler outrage taught perpetrators to conceal killings using poison and silence.

passage.bullet: Gold strikes at Ballarat and Bendigo drew 500,000 prospectors → tripled Australia’s population to 1.2 million
Free fortune-seekers from Europe, America, and China outnumbered convicts → reshaped colonial society
Vast gold exports funded railways, banks, and grand architecture → turned Melbourne into an imperial metropolis

context.bullet: Gold discoveries ended eastern convict transportation → Britain stopped shipping prisoners straight toward rich goldfields
Alluvial mining tore up Victorian creeks and sacred woodlands → devastated Indigenous lands a second time

stems.stem: Following Edward Hargraves’s 1851 find and huge strikes at ____________ and ____________, Australia’s population tripled to ____________.
Over half a million free prospectors arrived from ____________, ____________, and ____________, transforming a former penal society.
Surging bullion exports paid for railways and grand public buildings, making ____________ one of the Empire’s richest cities.

lesson_5.watch_out: Alluvial surface gold initially allowed ordinary diggers with pans and cradles to strike wealth, before deep-lead company mining took over.

passage.bullet: Every miner owed thirty shillings monthly even on empty shafts → bankrupted unlucky diggers
Corrupt troopers staged armed licence hunts → chained miners lacking paperwork directly to trees
Diggers paid heavy colonial taxes yet held zero voting rights → sparked Bakery Hill protests

context.bullet: Easy surface nuggets around Ballarat were running out by 1854 → made monthly fees unbearable
Many British and Irish miners brought Chartist reform ideals → framed grievances around democratic representation

stems.stem: Resentment boiled over because Victorian officials demanded a ____________ every month, even when diggers found ____________.
Corrupt troopers enforced the system through humiliating ____________, chaining unlicensed prospectors to trees.
Excluded from ____________, miners rallied at ____________ to protest paying heavy taxes without representation.

lesson_5.watch_out: Diggers were not simply dodging taxes—they protested corrupt police brutality and being denied parliamentary representation.

passage.bullet: Ballarat Reform League diggers built Eureka’s wooden palisade → swore allegiance beneath the Southern Cross flag
Nearly 300 redcoats crushed the stockade in fifteen minutes on 3 December → killed twenty-two miners
Melbourne juries acquitted rebel leaders → forced authorities to scrap licences and grant male suffrage

context.bullet: A cheap £1 annual Miner’s Right replaced the hated monthly fee → automatically carried voting rights
Victoria pioneered the printed secret ballot in 1856 → copied later by Britain and America

stems.stem: Swearing an oath beneath the ____________, Ballarat Reform League miners erected a timber barricade at Eureka.
Although British redcoats crushed the camp in a ____________ on 3 December 1854, killing ____________, public opinion backed the miners.
To restore calm, Victoria abolished ____________ and introduced landmark voting reforms including the ____________.

lesson_5.watch_out: Eureka was a swift military defeat for the miners, yet overwhelming public sympathy turned it into a political victory.

passage.bullet: Over 40,000 Chinese miners worked cooperatively on abandoned claims → sparked resentful white scapegoating
White mobs attacked Chinese camps at Lambing Flat in 1861 → drove colonial anti-Chinese entry taxes
Australia’s 1901 Parliament passed the Immigration Restriction Act → used rigged dictation tests to bar non-Europeans

context.bullet: White diggers who demanded democratic equality at Eureka → frequently backed racist laws excluding Asian workers
Officials gave dictation tests in unfamiliar European languages → ensured non-white applicants systematically failed

stems.stem: Envying the cooperative success of over 40,000 ____________, European prospectors accused them of wasting water and undercutting wages.
Racial hatred erupted during the 1861 ____________, where white crowds violently ransacked Chinese diggings.
At Federation in 1901, Parliament enshrined the ____________ through the ____________, using dictation tests to block non-European migrants.

lesson_5.watch_out: The 1901 dictation test was deliberately rigged—officials switched to obscure European languages so non-white migrants would fail.

passage.bullet: Federation denied Indigenous citizenship and enabled Stolen Generations child removals → entrenched systemic dispossession
Activists staged the 1938 Day of Mourning in Sydney → protested 150 years of dispossession
Eddie Mabo’s 1992 High Court victory recognised Native Title → demolished the myth of terra nullius

context.bullet: Colonial law had denied Indigenous ownership since Cook’s 1770 claim → Mabo reversed two centuries
Meriam people proved unbroken customary land inheritance on Murray Island → shattered old nomad stereotypes

stems.stem: Excluded from citizenship in 1901 and scarred by the ____________, Aboriginal activists protested during the 1938 ____________.
Decades of campaigning culminated in 1992 when the High Court’s ____________ decision formally recognised Indigenous ____________.
By acknowledging pre-existing customary law, the court finally overturned ____________ after more than two hundred years.

lesson_5.watch_out: Mabo did not grant new land from the Crown—the High Court recognised pre-existing Native Title that predated 1788.
